name: Control pause (CP) test

card.summary: A breath-hold timing used to track progress in nasal and reduced-volume breathing practice, which people pair with mouth-closed breathing routines aimed at a more relaxed, better-recovered look.
card.aka: BOLT score, Body Oxygen Level Test
card.note: Breath-holding is not advised for people with certain heart, lung or pregnancy conditions; the test is a self-measure rather than a diagnostic.

quick.overview:
The control pause (CP) is the number of seconds a person can comfortably hold their breath after a normal exhale, before the first clear urge to breathe. It comes from the Buteyko breathing method, and a close variant is popularized online as the BOLT (Body Oxygen Level Test) score. In looksmaxxing circles it serves as a scoreboard for nasal-breathing and mouth-taping routines, which proponents link to better sleep, calmer skin and facial posture.

Practitioners retest periodically and treat a rising number as a sign that their breathing practice is progressing. Published studies have mostly used the CP as an outcome measure in asthma and recovery research, while two recent papers have examined whether the BOLT score tracks fitness.
quick.how: People measure it seated and relaxed, usually in the morning, by timing a breath hold after a normal exhale and stopping at the first definite desire to breathe. They log the figure over weeks alongside practices such as nasal breathing, reduced-breathing exercises and mouth taping. Teachers of the Buteyko method say CP rises with practice over weeks to months.
quick.risks: The test itself is a brief breath hold, but practitioners and guidelines generally advise caution for people with serious heart conditions, uncontrolled asthma, panic disorder or pregnancy complications, and say to stop if dizzy. The CP is a self-reported timing, not a diagnostic, and its link to fitness or appearance outcomes has not been established.

lead: The control pause (CP) test is a simple breath-hold measurement: after a normal, relaxed exhale, a person pinches the nose and times how long they can hold before the first distinct urge to breathe. It originates in the Buteyko method, a breathing-retraining approach developed by the Soviet-era physiologist Konstantin Buteyko in the 1950s. [1] A near-identical version, the Body Oxygen Level Test (BOLT), is popular in fitness and breathwork circles. [2][3]

In looksmaxxing, the CP is used as a progress tracker for nasal breathing and related routines. Followers of these routines link steady nasal breathing to better sleep and recovery, a more rested face, and (in oral-posture communities) to jaw and tongue posture. A rising CP is treated as evidence that the breathing practice is working, which makes the number a motivational scoreboard.

Research on the CP has largely appeared in studies of the Buteyko technique in asthma, where it is recorded as an outcome alongside symptom scores. [4][5][6] Recent papers have asked whether BOLT/CP relates to athletic performance and aerobic fitness. [2][3] Whether the measure relates to facial appearance has not been studied.

angle.text: The CP is a measuring tool rather than a treatment: people use it to see whether nasal-breathing and mouth-taping routines are progressing. Those who practise them link the routines to better sleep and recovery, which show up in a rested appearance.

paras: The CP is the time from the end of a normal exhale until the first clear sign that breathing needs to resume, such as a first involuntary movement of the breathing muscles or a strong urge to inhale. Buteyko teachers distinguish it from a maximum breath hold, since the aim is a comfortable pause after which breathing resumes calmly. [1]
The BOLT score is the same idea marketed as a way to gauge tolerance to carbon dioxide and breathing efficiency, and is popular with breathwork coaches. [2][3]

Konstantin Buteyko developed the method in the 1950s, and it was studied at Leningrad in 1968 and at a Moscow paediatric institute in 1980 before spreading to Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States. [1] Buteyko teachers say practice raises the CP and lowers pulse rate, which they associate with fewer asthma symptoms. [1]

Social media interest rose in 2019 when the Indonesian singer Andien posted photos of herself and her family with tape over their mouths, which renewed attention on Buteyko-style nasal breathing. [1] The CP and BOLT numbers circulate in nasal-breathing and mouth-taping communities as the standard way to log progress.

Proponents hold that chronic over-breathing contributes to a range of problems and that a higher CP reflects more efficient breathing. Buteyko-method advocates say the method can reduce symptoms and medication reliance for asthma and related conditions, and some make claims about many other conditions. [1]
The researchers behind BOLT-focused studies note that its proponents describe it as reflecting sensitivity to carbon dioxide and giving feedback on exercise tolerance. [2][3]

A 2024 study in Frontiers in Physiology reported that BOLT was not associated with exercise performance in highly trained individuals. [2] A 2026 cross-sectional study of active university students examined associations between BOLT, VO2max, treadmill time to exhaustion and weekly physical activity. [3]

A British clinical guideline in 2014 said the Buteyko method might improve some asthma symptoms and quality of life in adults, with little effect on lung function, and a 2015 Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness. Researchers note that many studies are small and hard to blind, and that the hyperventilation theory lacks strong research support. [1]

The CP has been used as an outcome measure in small Buteyko trials. In a study of 40 adults with asthma, those given the Buteyko technique alongside medication were compared with a medication-only group. [4] A study of 33 school-age children with asthma at Mansoura University recorded the CP alongside asthma-control scores before and after training and reported improved control. [5][6] A small Indian study compared the Buteyko technique with incentive spirometry after coronary bypass surgery, using the CP as the breath-hold measure. [7] None of these tested appearance outcomes.
